analysis.title: Global Data Centers: New constraints (inflation, financing), but capacity growth still compelling
key_insights: MS forecasts global data center IT capacity growing +180 GW (+23% pa) from 2026e to 2030e, from ca 136 GW at end-2026e to ca 316 GW by 2030e. The US adds the most (+88 GW), then China (+49 GW), Europe (+12 GW), India (+7 GW), SE Asia (+6 GW) and the Middle East (+3 GW).

The report introduces bull and bear cases for the first time. Bull case: 377 GW by 2030e (+28% pa) if energy, planning, supply lines and construction ease. Bear case: 240 GW (+17% pa) if all Five Ps (Power, Planning, Price, People, Priority) are restrictive.

An AlphaWise survey of operators and suppliers in the US, China, UK, France and Spain finds energy is still the main bottleneck. Speed of access to electricity is the top bottleneck at 27% globally and 45% in the US. Chinese operators cite memory availability (29%) as the main constraint.
Over the next two years operators expect financing (14%) and access to water (17%) to rise in importance as bottlenecks. Speed of access to electricity stays #1 at 28%.

MS argues Price (build cost) is the next big debate after Power and Planning. Operators say total DC costs rose an average of +12% over the last 12 months and expect +15% pa over the next two years (US +17%, China +18%). Build cost per GW is projected to rise from $30bn (2022/23) to $50-60bn by the end of the decade.

If DC build inflation averages +8% pa to 2030 (slowing from +12% in 2026e to +5% in 2030e), total build cost rises about +50% in five years. MS sees the compounding effect as the main risk, and asks whether builders scale back capacity or accept higher capex.

MS projects a 70 GW US power shortfall for 2026-28 before 'time to power' solutions (BTM generation, turbines, powered shell providers, nuclear projects). Net of those it falls to 43 GW, and to 38 GW including APAC spillover. This is 33% of the power US developers need.

US developers are expected to look abroad for capacity: Europe, South Korea, Japan, India, SE Asia, Australia and the Middle East. MS estimates about +20 GW of excess non-China capacity could be exported to the US by 2030 in the base case, and +27 GW in the bull case.

AI-related credit issuance reached $471bn YTD through mid-October 2026, about 2.2x the $216bn issued in FY25. Credit markets are becoming more selective. High-quality hyperscalers (AMZN, MSFT, GOOGL, META) account for more than 75% of 2027E cash capex and can absorb higher funding costs.

Lower-rated hyperscalers and neoclouds face higher funding costs and may need secured asset-level financing or credit support from higher-quality players. CRWV unsecured debt trades above 1,000 bp, within 60bp of the CCC index, and the CDS AI basket trades more than 60bp wider than CDX IG.

MS says DC ABS supply is slowing as higher rates make ABS economics harder. New-issue DC ABS yields have spiked as Treasuries sold off and spreads widened. MS still forecasts gross ABS/CMBS issuance of $25-30bn in 2026, $40-50bn in 2027 and $55-65bn in 2028.

Modeled project returns are more sensitive to lease economics than to debt coupon and coverage assumptions. Developers controlling scarce powered sites can negotiate stronger lease terms. Investors are expected to require high-quality tenants, lower initial leverage and more amortization.

US community pushback is growing. About $156bn of projects were cancelled or delayed in 2025 and $130bn in 1Q26 alone. Gallup finds 70% of Americans oppose local DC construction. MS identified more than 250 delayed US projects, led by Georgia (3.0 GW), New Mexico (2.5 GW) and Louisiana (2.0 GW).

State actions in the US include a Pennsylvania executive order ending fast-track permitting, a New York one-year pause on state environmental permits for DCs of 50+ MW, a Texas audit of ERCOT interconnection requests (more than 474 GW pending) and the abandonment of the $25bn Digital Gateway project in Northern Virginia.

Europe is constrained but moving. The Irish moratorium ended with a December 2025 CRU policy requiring on-site generation and 80% additional renewable supply. Spain's draft Royal Decree would require 80% renewable matching, including hourly matching. Denmark placed DCs at the bottom of its grid queue. Scotland paused planning decisions for DCs above 50 MW.

US hyperscalers are expected to remain dominant in Europe. MS expects sovereign European DCs to be less than 10% of new build by 2035e, because customers are slow to switch and hyperscalers are adding 'Made in Europe' offerings. MS raised its 2035 Europe forecast about 15% to more than 40 GW. Europe bull/bear: 84 GW and 22 GW by 2035.

China is forecast to go from 26 GW in 2025 to 80 GW by 2030E, backed by Rmb8.5tr of cumulative capex. Power is not a bottleneck there. Domestic GPU shipments are forecast at 1.1mn (2025), 2.4mn (2026e) and 4.8mn (2027e), and HBM memory is the biggest constraint. China powershell cost is about US$3mn per MW against US$16mn in the US for GB300 deployment.

Memory is the newest inflation driver. Memory prices have risen more than 6x in the past year, and TrendForce sees the memory market going from about $220bn in 2025 to about $890bn in 2026. MS calls it a structural reset driven by AI demand for HBM and DRAM.

India capacity is forecast to rise from about 1.8 GW (FY26e) to 10.5 GW (FY31e), implying about US$70bn of investment at US$6-10mn per MW. South Korea has about 5 GW of announced plans and a base case of about +2 GW. Australia is forecast to grow from 1.8 GW to 6.1 GW by 2030 (+31% CAGR).

US stock implications: Overweight on powered shell providers CIFR, HUT, RIOT, GLXY and WULF, Equal-weight APLD and Underweight MARA. Overweight BEs, GEV and CMI for BTM power equipment. Overweight EQIX (preferred) and CSQR in colocation, Equal-weight DLR. A balanced view on CoreWeave and Nebius because of execution risk and capital-raising uncertainty.

Natural gas pipeline stocks are called the most attractive value in midstream. WMB is Overweight and Top Pick with a $103 fair value. DTM and TRP are Overweight. The stocks have lagged on state-level DC pushback, onsite power cost concerns and higher long-dated yields.

SpaceX (SPCX) is seen as a leader in scaling time-to-power solutions. MS identifies 3-4 GW of likely accessible gas turbine power by YE27 and sees terrestrial compute peaking at about 25 GW in 2031. The practical constraint is turbine blades and vanes.

European sector views: MERLIN (Top Pick, Overweight) trades at a 27% discount to NAV, with risk from the Spanish draft decree and tenant concentration (neoclouds about 85% of DC rent). Utilities preferred plays are RWE and EDP. In capital goods, Legrand is Top Pick (about 6% upside to consensus 2027 EBIT), Siemens Energy is Overweight and Wartsila is Underweight.

Euro area DC capex of about €34bn in 2026 and €56bn in 2027 is worth 0.2pp and 0.3pp of GDP, but the real growth impact is less than half of that given import content (more than 50 cents of each euro goes to NVIDIA). The UK is modeled at about a 30bp average capex boost to growth in 2026-27.

earnings_insights: Siemens Energy reports FY26 results and new 2030 targets on 11 Nov 2026 (MS Overweight). MS sees a possible entry point ahead of the event.
MS expects Legrand to possibly raise its organic growth guidance in 3Q26. Legrand updated its DC FY27-30 organic revenue CAGR to mid to high teens.

In 1H26 results, Schneider, ABB and Siemens said DC-related order growth was in the 'triple digits', and Legrand said about 30%. Vertiv's Americas organic revenue growth was above 40% over the last 12 months.
2Q26 gas turbine orders were a record 38GW, annualizing at 134GW in 1H26. MS thinks 2026 is the peak and the debate is how far orders moderate in 2027.
MS is 5.4% and 5.1% above value-added EBIT consensus for 2027 at Schneider and Legrand respectively.
Merlin said at its 1H26 results call (July) that 160MW was let or pre-let, with another 180MW in Lisbon in advanced negotiations. CoreWeave is 9% of Merlin's total rents.

risk_factors: Power and grid access remain the main bottleneck, especially in the US where the net shortfall is 38-43 GW through 2028.
DC build cost inflation of about 15% pa could compound to a roughly 50% cost increase over five years and weigh on development yields.
Credit markets are becoming more selective. Neoclouds and lower-rated hyperscalers face higher funding costs, and CRWV unsecured debt trades above 1,000 bp.
Higher global interest rates are slowing DC securitized credit supply.
US community opposition and state and local moratoriums are growing, with 250+ projects delayed.
Memory (HBM, DRAM) price spikes and shortages, especially in China.
Possible pre- or double-ordering behind the surge in electrical equipment and gas turbine orders. 2026 may be the peak for gas turbine orders.
Hyperscalers may slow rollout if AI returns on capital (ROCE) are lower than expected.
Regulatory risk in Europe from Spain's draft Royal Decree, Denmark's grid priority change and Scottish planning pauses.
Middle East security risk after recent regional military conflict.
Possible oversupply in South Korea, with capacity additions concentrated around 2029-30.
charts_described: Exhibit 5 shows US power needed 2026-28 of 116 GW, less 25 GW of DCs under construction (FTM+BTM) and 21 GW of available grid, leaving a potential 70 GW shortfall.
Exhibit 11 plots global DC capacity: base case 136 GW (2026e) to 316 GW (2030e), bull case 377 GW and bear case 240 GW.
Exhibit 8 shows YTD-26 global credit issuance of $471bn versus $132bn YTD-25 and $216bn in FY25. HQ hyperscalers in USD were $132bn.
Exhibit 46 shows CRWV unsecured spreads above 1,000 bp, close to the CCC index OAS.
Exhibit 133 shows 2Q26 gas turbine orders of 38GW, a record above the year-2000 quarterly peaks.
vol_and_positioning: Natural gas pipeline stocks have underperformed in recent months. MS sees entry points in the pullback, with new project announcements as catalysts through year-end.
Short-term correlations of Canadian midstream names (ENB, TRP) to the 10-year yield tend to spike to around -0.5 around the onset of a Fed hiking cycle, roughly twice the level for US peers.
EU Cap Goods data center valuation discount to US is -18% on 1-year forward EV/EBIT, well below the May 2026 peak discount of -27%.
Siemens trades on 19.3x 2027e P/E, Legrand on 19.8x and Siemens Energy on 20.4x.
geopolitical: US federal permitting executive order (July 2025) to accelerate DC approvals, against rising state and local moratoriums.
US export restrictions on Nvidia's most advanced GPUs (Hopper, Blackwell) to China under a presumption-of-denial policy, with a possible approval of the RTX 5500Pro reported.
Recent regional military conflict in the Middle East has raised security concerns, with DCs targeted.
European data sovereignty push (Draghi report, EU digital sovereignty summit) versus the US CLOUD Act and the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
Import tariffs on electronic equipment raising US DC capital goods costs.

Scotland, Denmark, Spain, Greece and France are acting on DC grid and planning rules, including a French parliamentary commission recommendation of a moratorium on projects that do not serve digital sovereignty.

tension_points.bull_case: MS base case sees +23% pa growth to 316 GW by 2030e. Bull case 377 GW if energy, planning and supply constraints ease. 99% of operators are confident of meeting 2030 targets, 47% of US capacity is pre-leased and US contract pricing is up about 12% year on year.
tension_points.bear_case: Bear case of 240 GW if all Five Ps restrict. More than 250 US projects are delayed, with a 38-43 GW net US power shortfall, 15% pa cost inflation and a growing risk of moratoriums.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Restrictions across all Five Ps (energy, planning, price, people, priority) would take capacity growth to the 240 GW bear case.

tension_points.bull_case: HQ hyperscalers (AMZN, MSFT, GOOGL, META) are about AA rated, have market caps above $3 trillion, and account for more than 75% of 2027E capex. They can absorb higher funding costs, and plenty of capital remains.
tension_points.bear_case: Lower-rated hyperscalers and neoclouds face rising funding costs. CRWV debt trades above 1,000 bp, DC ABS supply is slowing and the CDS AI basket is more than 60bp wider than CDX IG.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Continued spread widening and higher rates that stop lower-quality issuers from raising capital would change the timing, structure or scale of investment.

tension_points.bull_case: DC-related orders at Schneider, ABB and Siemens are growing triple digits, with 2027 EBIT estimates seen as too low and a favorable price/cost setup.
tension_points.bear_case: Orders may include pre- or double-ordering, and the right normalised order level is unclear. Gas turbine orders may have peaked in 2026.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A moderation in gas turbine orders in 2027, or DC build constraints that hit pricing per MW.
